prompt.context: Telco Towers is a cell tower company in the United States which leases space on its towers to wireless providers (i.e. AT&T, Verizon, etc.) who install their respective antennas / technology on its towers. With the advent, and expansion, of 5G across the country, Telco Towers is locked into a contract to upgrade its suite of towers to support 5G technology and now needs a strategy to grow its business to cover the cost of upgrading its towers.
prompt.question: How should Telco Towers grow its business to cover the cost of upgrading its towers to support 5G technology?

clarifying_info.q: What is Telco Towers' current revenue model?
clarifying_info.a: Leasing space on its towers to wireless providers is currently Telco Towers' sole form of revenue. Rental space is charged per antenna installed by the lessee.

The market is fragmented overall with new competitors entering the market and providing rental space on towers for a fraction of Telco Towers' price, eroding margins. Wireless providers are also pursuing their own tower builds to minimize costs.

clarifying_info.q: How many towers does Telco Towers have?
clarifying_info.a: Telco Towers has approximately 20,000 towers across the United States.

clarifying_info.q: Can Telco Towers renegotiate the upgrade contracts?
clarifying_info.a: The contracts and costs to upgrade the towers have already been signed and are therefore not negotiable at this point.

clarifying_info.q: How does the antenna pricing work?
clarifying_info.a: Each antenna can support service to a certain number of households, so at times the lessee needs multiple antennas to support service to all of its customers in a given area.

exhibits.title: Potential New Customers in Telco Tower's Footprint
exhibits.shows: A table or chart listing several telecom/broadband companies, their total user bases, and the percentage of those users who fall within Telco Tower's geographic footprint.
exhibits.data: Blue Devil Broadband: 60M total users, 50% in footprint; NC Communications: 50M total users, 40% in footprint; Duke Wireless: 30M total users, 95% in footprint; Tar Heel Broadband: 15M total users, 20% in footprint; 27701 Wireless: 14M total users, 30% in footprint

framework: Revenues — Existing Business: adjust pricing on current leases; sign current customers to leases on other towers; extend term of existing contracts

Revenues — New Business: identify new customers (wireless providers not yet on Telco Towers); identify new use cases where businesses may need tower space (e.g., Fixed Wireless Access broadband providers)
Costs — Fixed: salaries, utilities, rent, property taxes, expense of upgrading towers to 5G
Interviewer note: de-prioritize costs in the framework because the upgrade expense is already contracted and non-negotiable; focus should be on new business revenue opportunities

questions.prompt: Which potential new customer represents the largest revenue opportunity within Telco Tower's footprint, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the number of users inside Telco Tower's footprint for each company (total users × % in footprint), identify Blue Devil Broadband as the largest opportunity (30M users), and recognize it is a start-up providing 5G fixed broadband to households — a new use case for Telco Towers. Candidate should proactively ask for additional data needed to size the revenue opportunity.

math.setup: Users in footprint = Total users × % in footprint. Then convert users to households, households to antennas, antennas to monthly revenue, and monthly to annual revenue.
steps: Blue Devil Broadband: 50% × 60M = 30M users in footprint
Tar Heel Broadband: 20% × 15M = 3M users in footprint
Blue Devil Broadband is largest (30M users); select it for full sizing
math.answer: Pursuing a tower rental arrangement with Blue Devil Broadband represents approximately $90M in annual revenue.

brainstorming.prompt: What non-financial factors should we consider when evaluating a potential partnership with these companies?

categories.name: Business Viability
ideas: Viability of each company's business model (start-ups like Blue Devil Broadband carry higher risk than established players)
Likelihood that the company survives long enough to justify investment in the partnership

categories.name: Competitive Dynamics
ideas: Likelihood of winning the partnership over cheaper competitors
Share of business Telco Towers is likely to win (e.g., 95% share with Duke Wireless vs. only 50% share with Blue Devil Broadband?)
Price competitiveness of Telco Towers' $1,500/month/antenna rate vs. market

categories.name: Relationships & Access
ideas: Existing connections and relationships with each potential partner company
Ease of scheduling and reaching decision-makers at each firm

categories.name: Operational Capacity
ideas: Rental capacity available on existing towers — sufficient to service the new customer's antenna requirements?
Impact on quality of service to existing customers if new customers increase tower utilization

recommendation: Telco Towers should pursue a lessor/lessee partnership with Blue Devil Broadband, which represents the largest revenue opportunity (~$90M/year) within Telco Tower's footprint.

Telco Towers should simultaneously consider pursuing similar arrangements with Duke Wireless and/or NC Communications, assuming sufficient tower capacity exists, to diversify and maximize revenue growth.
risks: Decrease in quality of service to existing customers due to increased tower usage from new customers
Loss of the RFP/partnership proposal to a cheaper competitor in the marketplace
next_steps: Schedule a meeting with leadership at Blue Devil Broadband (and possibly Duke Wireless and/or NC Communications)
Test the reasonability of Telco Towers' monthly pricing ($1,500 per antenna) against competitors to ensure a competitive offering
